passage: Okay, so for my first month I kept a private list of who sat next to whom in the weekly meeting, Ritu. I am Kalyani, and I thought the sales head had a favourite because the same colleague always sat at his right hand. I also noticed the new hire always chose the end chair, and I decided he was shy or afraid. I nearly told a friend that story. Then I learned the right-hand chair was closest to the projector cable, and the end seat had the only working socket. Habit and logistics, not rank. I stopped guessing. If seating does mean something, it will show in how people are actually treated over time.

qa.q: Why did the same colleague sit at the sales head's right hand?
qa.a: That chair was closest to the projector cable.

qa.q: What did Kalyani first think about the seats, and what changed that view?
qa.a: Kalyani first thought the seating showed favouritism and fear, but learned it was logistics like the cable and the socket. Seating can reflect rank, but here the evidence pointed elsewhere.

qa.q: What would you advise Kalyani about reading seating in the future?
qa.a: Kalyani can look at how people are treated over time and check facts before guessing at hidden meaning.

qa.q: How might the new hire have felt about Kalyani's private list?
qa.a: The new hire may have been unaware, and would probably feel misjudged if told the end chair meant fear when it was about the socket.

grounding: Spoken monologue on a young professional reading seating and distance in meetings, learning it can be habit or logistics.

passage: I sit near Nirmala in the office in Dharamshala and I notice things. On Monday, Tenzin, the new manager, took the chair at the long table's corner instead of the head, and Nirmala took the seat farthest from him. Two colleagues made a show of sitting close beside Tenzin. I could not tell whether anyone meant anything by it. Later Nirmala said the far chair had the only window and the only fan. Tenzin, when I asked lightly, said the corner chair was where the light was best for reading. I think I was wrong to read a story into it at first. People's positions can be rank, comfort or just where the fan is.

qa.q: Where did Tenzin sit at the long table?
qa.a: Tenzin took the chair at the corner.

qa.q: What might the narrator have been thinking about the seating at first, and what changed that?
qa.a: The narrator suspected the seats showed rank and distance, but learned Nirmala's chair had the only window and fan, and Tenzin's had the best light. The seating was about comfort.

qa.q: What could the narrator do next time before guessing at meaning?
qa.a: The narrator could ask lightly, as was done with Tenzin, or watch how people behave over time.

qa.q: How might Nirmala have felt about being seen as distant?
qa.a: Nirmala may have been surprised, since the seat was chosen for the window and fan and not for distance.

grounding: Observer's account of a young professional reading seating in a meeting as status, learning it can be habit or logistics.
